## As R.E.M. ascended from scrappy college rock beginnings to arenas, they achieved global stardom on their own terms. Morphing from chiming folk rock to mandolin-driven radio pop to singalong stadium anthems, their outsider status remained intact, their collaborative band identity solid. In every aspect of their journey, the band created an alt-rock template that inspired both artists and legions of fans worldwide.

## Melodic, Introspective Alt Rock

R.E.M. burst from early ‘80s Athens, GA, with a distinctive mix of jangle-pop guitar, propulsive rhythms, intriguing, inscrutable vocals, and a renowned live show. Evolving into a ‘90s and ‘00s arena act, they added synth, fuzz guitar, power ballads and anthems aplenty, remaining both accessible and slyly innovative.

## Rhinestoned R.E.M.

Bassist Mike Mills first donned a rhinestoned “Nudie suit” in 1994 during R.E.M.’s Monster tour. He then commissioned a series of lavish ensembles from foremost Western designer Manuel (previously Nudie’s head designer), who created this jacket (with matching pants).

“When you put one of these suits on,” said Mills, “you become a different person, but I tend to be that when I walk out onstage anyway.”

## As R.E.M. ascended from scrappy college rock beginnings to arenas, they achieved global stardom on their own terms. Morphing from chiming folk rock to mandolin-driven radio pop to singalong stadium anthems, their outsider status remained intact, their collaborative band identity solid. In every aspect of their journey, the band created an alt-rock template that inspired both artists and legions of fans worldwide.

## Melodic, Introspective Alt Rock

R.E.M. burst from early ‘80s Athens, GA, with a distinctive mix of jangle-pop guitar, propulsive rhythms, intriguing, inscrutable vocals, and a renowned live show. Evolving into a ‘90s and ‘00s arena act, they added synth, fuzz guitar, power ballads and anthems aplenty, remaining both accessible and slyly innovative.

## Rhinestoned R.E.M.

Bassist Mike Mills first donned a rhinestoned “Nudie suit” in 1994 during R.E.M.’s Monster tour. He then commissioned a series of lavish ensembles from foremost Western designer Manuel (previously Nudie’s head designer), who created this jacket (with matching pants).

“When you put one of these suits on,” said Mills, “you become a different person, but I tend to be that when I walk out onstage anyway.”

Not to be confused with [Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Melle_Mel_and_the_Furious_Five "Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five").

"Furious Five" redirects here. For other uses, see [Furious 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furious_5_(disambiguation) "Furious 5 (disambiguation)").

**Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five** were an American [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") group formed in the [South Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx "South Bronx") of New York City in 1978. The group's members were [Grandmaster Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash "Grandmaster Flash"), [Kidd Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidd_Creole "Kidd Creole") (not to be confused with [Kid Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_Creole "Kid Creole")), [Keef Cowboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keef_Cowboy "Keef Cowboy"), [Melle Mel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melle_Mel "Melle Mel"), Scorpio and Rahiem. The group's use of [turntablism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turntablism "Turntablism"), [breakbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakbeat "Breakbeat") DJing and [conscious lyricism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_hip_hop#Conscious_hip_hop "Political hip hop") were significant in the early development of hip hop music.

In the late 1970s, Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five built their reputation and achieved local success by performing at parties and live shows. By 1980, the group had signed with [Sugar Hill Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Hill_Records_(hip_hop_label) "Sugar Hill Records (hip hop label)"), but it was not until the release of the song "[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five song)")" in 1982 and the album [_The Message_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_album) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five album)") that they achieved mainstream success. The song provided a [political](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_criticism "Political criticism") and [social commentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_commentary "Social commentary") and went on to become a driving force behind [conscious hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscious_hip-hop "Conscious hip-hop").

Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five split into two separate groups in 1983 until a brief reunion in 1987 led to the release of the original line-up's second album _[On the Strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Strength "On the Strength")_. Afterwards, they disbanded permanently. Today, the group's legacy continues as **Grandmaster's Furious Five** with only Melle Mel and Scorpio as remaining members.

Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five were inducted into the [Rock & Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") in 2007, the first hip hop group to be inducted.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2) They have been ranked as one of the greatest rap groups of all time by _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_ (2023).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-3) In 2002, "The Message" was one of the 50 inaugural recordings chosen by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") to be added to the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-5)_[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked "The Message" number 59 on its list of the [500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time") in 2021.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-6)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Formation and early years (1978–1979)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formation and early years (1978–1979)")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Flier_for_a_rap_battle_in_the_Bronx.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Flier_for_a_rap_battle_in_the_Bronx.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flier_for_a_rap_battle_in_the_Bronx.tif)

1979 Bronx Rap Battle. Design: Buddy Esquire. Image courtesy of Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture

Prior to the formation of the Furious Five, Grandmaster Flash worked with the "L Brothers", which consisted of "Mean Gene" Livingston, Claudio Livingston and [Grand Wizzard Theodore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Wizzard_Theodore "Grand Wizzard Theodore").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-7) Flash then recruited his friend [Cowboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keef_Cowboy "Keef Cowboy"), Melle Mel and Kidd Creole (Nathaniel Glover).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-nyt-creole-murder-8) The trio called themselves the Three MC's, forming the first emcee group as it relates to [rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rap "Rap") as it is known today. Cowboy performed a "scat routine" at a party (at "The Black Door") for a friend who had just joined the U.S. Army. He began [scat singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scat_singing "Scat singing") the words "hip/hop/hip/hop" in a way that mimicked the [rhythmic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm") cadence of the U.S. Army marching drill.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-youtube.com-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-furious5-10) He then worked the "hip hop" cadence into part of his performance. This led to the term "hip hoppers" being used derogatorily by the culture's early detractors, most of whom were from the disco set, to label the music used. This evolved into the term "Hip Hop" and was later adopted by the industry.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-youtube.com-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-furious5-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-11)

Melle Mel and Kidd Creole were the first rappers to call themselves "MCs" (Masters of Ceremonies). The 3 emcees worked with Flash, who went on to bring in Scorpio and Rahiem (Guy Todd Williams). After the formation of the Furious 5, Flash also worked with rapper [Kurtis Blow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtis_Blow "Kurtis Blow") doing parties in Queens. During the time Flash worked with Kurtis Blow, it was mainly due to internal disputes with the emcees, so for a short time prior to the formation of the [Cold Crush Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_Crush_Brothers "Cold Crush Brothers") in 1979, DJ Charlie Chase was the Furious 5's DJ.

Grandmaster Flash & The Furious 5 were the number one rap group on the streets of New York City before rap music was embraced by the music industry, setting the standard for all other emcee groups who came after them. The first single they released was "We Rap More Mellow", which was registered under the name _The Younger Generation_. The name change was made by the producer, who considered it better.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-12)

The group was popular locally, gaining recognition for their skillful raps and deejaying, but it was not until the [Sugarhill Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarhill_Gang "Sugarhill Gang")'s "[Rapper's Delight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapper's_Delight "Rapper's Delight")" proved that hip hop music could achieve mainstream success that they began recording. In 1979, they released their first single on [Enjoy Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enjoy_Records "Enjoy Records"), "Superappin". The group went on to sign with [Sylvia Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Robinson "Sylvia Robinson")'s [Sugar Hill Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Hill_Records_(rap) "Sugar Hill Records (rap)"), following an agreement that they could perform over a then-popular DJ favorite.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

### Mainstream success and _The Message_ (1980–1982)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mainstream success and The Message (1980–1982)")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/25/Grandmaster_Flash_and_The_Furious_Five_Promotional.jpg/250px-Grandmaster_Flash_and_The_Furious_Five_Promotional.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grandmaster_Flash_and_The_Furious_Five_Promotional.jpg)

1980 promotional still of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five on mainstream success

In 1980, the group released their Sugarhill Records debut, "Freedom", which reached #19 on the R&B chart and sold over 50,000 copies.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-Grandmaster_Flash_Biography-15) The follow-up, "Birthday Party" was also a hit.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-Grandmaster_Flash_Biography-15) In 1981, Grandmaster Flash released _[The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Adventures\_of\_Grandmaster\_Flash\_on\_the\_Wheels\_of\_Steel "The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel")_, which was a multi-deck, live recording of one of his routines that featured [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(band) "Queen (band)")'s "[Another One Bites the Dust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Another_One_Bites_the_Dust "Another One Bites the Dust")" and [Chic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chic_(band) "Chic (band)")'s "[Good Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Times_(Chic_song) "Good Times (Chic song)")". The release marked the first time that scratching & turntablism were featured on a record.

In 1982, the group released "[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five song)")", which was produced by [Clifton "Jiggs" Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton_%22Jiggs%22_Chase "Clifton \"Jiggs\" Chase") and Ed "Duke Bootee" Fletcher, the latter of whom wrote the song (Sylvia Robinson added Melle Mel's rhyme from an earlier song to complete the recording). It provided a [political](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_criticism "Political criticism") and [social commentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_commentary "Social commentary") and went on to become a driving force behind [conscious hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscious_hip-hop "Conscious hip-hop"). The song peaked at #4 in the R&B chart and #62 in the pop chart, and established hip-hop's credibility in mainstream music. Other than Melle Mel, however, no members of the group (except for background vocals at the end) actually feature on the record.

Their debut album, also named _[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Message\_(Grandmaster\_Flash\_and\_the\_Furious\_Five\_album) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five album)")_, went on to become a prominent achievement in the history of hip-hop.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

### Breakup (1983–1986)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Breakup (1983–1986)")]

In 1983, Grandmaster Flash, who had never appeared on any of the group's studio recordings, sued Sugar Hill Records for $5 million in unpaid royalties. This resulted in the single "[White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Lines_(Don't_Don't_Do_It) "White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)")" being credited to "Grandmaster & Melle Mel." The song reached #47 in [_Billboard_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")'s[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_R&B/Hip-Hop_Songs "Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs") chart. Another lawsuit was filed over certain elements of the song being stolen from "Cavern" by [Liquid Liquid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Liquid "Liquid Liquid"), from which Sugar Hill Records would never recover.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-16)

The royalties dispute split the group. Melle Mel, Scorpio and Cowboy left after "White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)" was a hit. They formed Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five and released the album _Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five_ in 1984. Meanwhile, Grandmaster Flash, Kidd Creole and Rahiem left for [Elektra Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elektra_Records "Elektra Records") and added three new members to the group: Kevin "The Lord LaVon" Dukes, Russell "Mr. Broadway" Wheeler and "Larry-Love" Parker. They worked under the name "Grandmaster Flash" on _[They Said It Couldn't Be Done](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/They\_Said\_It\_Couldn't\_Be\_Done "They Said It Couldn't Be Done")_, _[The Source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Source\_(Grandmaster\_Flash\_album) "The Source (Grandmaster Flash album)")_ and _[Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang "Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang")_. The additional members The Lord La Von, Larry Love and Mr. Broadway formed the "Furious Five" but they could not use the name as Sugar Hill Records owned the rights.

Grandmaster Flash and his new "Furious Five" had a few hits with their three albums that made it to the top fifty of _Billboard_'s [R&B/Hip-Hop Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_R&B/Hip-Hop_Albums "Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums") chart, whereas [Melle Mel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melle_Mel "Melle Mel") and his group fared better. Grandmaster Melle Mel's most notable hit was "Beat Street Breakdown", which peaked at #8 in the R&B chart. Melle Mel also appeared in [Chaka Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaka_Khan "Chaka Khan")'s "[I Feel for You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Feel_for_You "I Feel for You")", which won the [Grammy Award for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Female_R&B_Vocal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance") in 1985.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

### Reunion and waning popularity (1987–1988)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reunion and waning popularity (1987–1988)")]

In 1987, the original lineup of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five reformed for a performance at a charity concert at Madison Square Garden. They soon reunited for their first studio album in nearly five years, recording _[On the Strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Strength "On the Strength")_, which was released in April 1988. Reception of the album was lukewarm, and it failed to achieve the same levels of success as _[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Message\_(Grandmaster\_Flash\_and\_the\_Furious\_Five\_album) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five album)")_. The group never enjoyed the same success as they did in the early 1980s and permanently broke up afterwards.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

### Permanent disbandment and post-_On the Strength_ (1989–2022)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Permanent disbandment and post-On the Strength (1989–2022)")]

Since disbanding, some members of the group have briefly worked together. Melle Mel, Scorpio and Cowboy released another album as Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five, _Piano_, in 1989. Keith "Cowboy" Wiggins died on September 8, 1989.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-17)

In 1990, Grandmaster Flash produced Just-Ice's album _[Masterpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterpiece\_(Just-Ice\_album) "Masterpiece (Just-Ice album)")_. He went on to work as musical director for _[The Chris Rock Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Chris\_Rock\_Show "The Chris Rock Show")_, and later released _[The Official Adventures of Grandmaster Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Official\_Adventures\_of\_Grandmaster\_Flash "The Official Adventures of Grandmaster Flash")_, _[Essential Mix: Classic Edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential\_Mix:\_Classic\_Edition "Essential Mix: Classic Edition")_ and _[The Bridge (Concept of a Culture)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bridge\_(Concept\_of\_a\_Culture) "The Bridge (Concept of a Culture)")_. He has also received many accolades, including the DJ Vanguard Award from [Bill Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates") in 2004, [RIAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA "RIAA")'s Lifetime Achievement Award at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum in 2005, and [BET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BET "BET")'s [I Am Hip-Hop Icon Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BET_Hip_Hop_Awards#2006_BET_Hip_Hop_Awards_winners "BET Hip Hop Awards") in 2006. His autobiography, _The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash: My Life, My Beats_, was released in 2008.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-18)

In 1985, Melle Mel met [Quincy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Jones "Quincy Jones") at the Grammys, and they began to collaborate for _[Back on the Block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back\_on\_the\_Block "Back on the Block")_. This led to Mel being featured in the song "Back on the Block", which won him the [Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rap_Performance_by_a_Duo_or_Group "Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group") in 1991. He would pick up an additional [Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Spoken_Word_Album "Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album") in 2002 for his contributions in _Q: The Autobiography of Quincy Jones._ 1997 saw him sign onto Straight Game Records and release _[Right Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right\_Now\_(Melle\_Mel\_album) "Right Now (Melle Mel album)")_ with Mr. Ness/Scorpio. The album also featured Rondo; the two went on to form a group called _Die Hard_. In 2012, they released an album titled _On Lock_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-interview-19)

On January 23, 2007, Mel changed his name to Grandmaster Melle Mel and released his first solo studio album, _[Muscles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscles\_(album) "Muscles (album)")_. The first single and music video was "M3 – The New Message". He has also released the children's book _The Portal in the Park_, which features a CD on which children can read and rap along with him. This project featured a then-unknown [Lady Gaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Gaga "Lady Gaga"). She performs with Mel on the songs "World Family Tree" and "The Fountain Of Truth".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

When asked of a possible reunion in 2002, Melle Mel responded:

> It['s] not a question of whether we could get together or not [...] I just don['t] think that we could get a deal. The record company people just don['t] see a market for us.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-interview-19)

However, 2014 saw Melle Mel and Scorpio begin playing shows across the United States, UK and Europe as Grandmaster's Furious Five ft Melle [sic] and Scorpio, culminating in them writing and recording new music. Their first single 'Some Kind of Sorry' was released on May 27, 2016,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-Jammerzine-20) to coincide with a UK and European tour, which they are undertaking alongside [The Sugarhill Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sugarhill_Gang "The Sugarhill Gang").

On August 2, 2017, Nathaniel Glover (Kidd Creole) was arrested and charged with the murder of a New York city homeless man.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-nyt-creole-murder-8)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-22) In 2022, Glover was found guilty of manslaughter in relation to the case, and was sentenced to sixteen years in prison.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-24)

## Legacy and influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legacy and influence")]

Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five are a well-respected group in the history of hip-hop music. They have been honored at the VH1 Hip Hop Honors in 2005 and were inducted into the [Rock & Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_&_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock & Roll Hall of Fame") in 2007. The Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. displays in their historical archives the vinyl records and the turntable used by DJ Grandmaster Flash.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-25) In 2021, they received their first [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") for [lifetime achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award"), becoming the second hip-hop act to receive the Grammy after [Run-DMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run-DMC "Run-DMC").

They have influenced many musical acts[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-26) such as [Anthony Kiedis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Kiedis "Anthony Kiedis"), [New Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Order_(band) "New Order (band)"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-27)[The Cold Crush Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cold_Crush_Brothers "The Cold Crush Brothers"), [Run-D.M.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run-D.M.C. "Run-D.M.C."), [Whodini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whodini "Whodini"), [Public Enemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Enemy_(group) "Public Enemy (group)"), [Boogie Down Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogie_Down_Productions "Boogie Down Productions"), [KRS-One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KRS-One "KRS-One"), [EPMD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EPMD "EPMD"), [Stetsasonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stetsasonic "Stetsasonic"), [Doug E. American hip hop group (1978–1988)

Not to be confused with [Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Melle_Mel_and_the_Furious_Five "Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five").

**Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five** were an American [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") group formed in the [South Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx "South Bronx") of New York City in 1978. The group's members were [Grandmaster Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash "Grandmaster Flash"), [Kidd Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidd_Creole "Kidd Creole") (not to be confused with [Kid Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_Creole "Kid Creole")), [Keef Cowboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keef_Cowboy "Keef Cowboy"), [Melle Mel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melle_Mel "Melle Mel"), Scorpio and Rahiem. The group's use of [turntablism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turntablism "Turntablism"), [breakbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakbeat "Breakbeat") DJing and [conscious lyricism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_hip_hop#Conscious_hip_hop "Political hip hop") were significant in the early development of hip hop music.

In the late 1970s, Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five built their reputation and achieved local success by performing at parties and live shows. By 1980, the group had signed with [Sugar Hill Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Hill_Records_(hip_hop_label) "Sugar Hill Records (hip hop label)"), but it was not until the release of the song "[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five song)")" in 1982 and the album [_The Message_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_album) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five album)") that they achieved mainstream success. The song provided a [political](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_criticism "Political criticism") and [social commentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_commentary "Social commentary") and went on to become a driving force behind [conscious hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscious_hip-hop "Conscious hip-hop").

Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five split into two separate groups in 1983 until a brief reunion in 1987 led to the release of the original line-up's second album _[On the Strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Strength "On the Strength")_. Afterwards, they disbanded permanently. Today, the group's legacy continues as **Grandmaster's Furious Five** with only Melle Mel and Scorpio as remaining members.

Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five were inducted into the [Rock & Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") in 2007, the first hip hop group to be inducted.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2) They have been ranked as one of the greatest rap groups of all time by _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_ (2023).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-3) In 2002, "The Message" was one of the 50 inaugural recordings chosen by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") to be added to the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-5)_[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked "The Message" number 59 on its list of the [500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time") in 2021.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-6)

### Formation and early years (1978–1979)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formation and early years (1978–1979)")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Flier_for_a_rap_battle_in_the_Bronx.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Flier_for_a_rap_battle_in_the_Bronx.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flier_for_a_rap_battle_in_the_Bronx.tif)

1979 Bronx Rap Battle. Design: Buddy Esquire. Image courtesy of Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture

Prior to the formation of the Furious Five, Grandmaster Flash worked with the "L Brothers", which consisted of "Mean Gene" Livingston, Claudio Livingston and [Grand Wizzard Theodore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Wizzard_Theodore "Grand Wizzard Theodore").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-7) Flash then recruited his friend [Cowboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keef_Cowboy "Keef Cowboy"), Melle Mel and Kidd Creole (Nathaniel Glover).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-nyt-creole-murder-8) The trio called themselves the Three MC's, forming the first emcee group as it relates to [rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rap "Rap") as it is known today. Cowboy performed a "scat routine" at a party (at "The Black Door") for a friend who had just joined the U.S. Army. He began [scat singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scat_singing "Scat singing") the words "hip/hop/hip/hop" in a way that mimicked the [rhythmic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm "Rhythm") cadence of the U.S. Army marching drill.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-youtube.com-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-furious5-10) He then worked the "hip hop" cadence into part of his performance. This led to the term "hip hoppers" being used derogatorily by the culture's early detractors, most of whom were from the disco set, to label the music used. This evolved into the term "Hip Hop" and was later adopted by the industry.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-youtube.com-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-furious5-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-11)

Melle Mel and Kidd Creole were the first rappers to call themselves "MCs" (Masters of Ceremonies). The 3 emcees worked with Flash, who went on to bring in Scorpio and Rahiem (Guy Todd Williams). After the formation of the Furious 5, Flash also worked with rapper [Kurtis Blow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtis_Blow "Kurtis Blow") doing parties in Queens. During the time Flash worked with Kurtis Blow, it was mainly due to internal disputes with the emcees, so for a short time prior to the formation of the [Cold Crush Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_Crush_Brothers "Cold Crush Brothers") in 1979, DJ Charlie Chase was the Furious 5's DJ.

Grandmaster Flash & The Furious 5 were the number one rap group on the streets of New York City before rap music was embraced by the music industry, setting the standard for all other emcee groups who came after them. The first single they released was "We Rap More Mellow", which was registered under the name _The Younger Generation_. The name change was made by the producer, who considered it better.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-12)

The group was popular locally, gaining recognition for their skillful raps and deejaying, but it was not until the [Sugarhill Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugarhill_Gang "Sugarhill Gang")'s "[Rapper's Delight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapper's_Delight "Rapper's Delight")" proved that hip hop music could achieve mainstream success that they began recording. In 1979, they released their first single on [Enjoy Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enjoy_Records "Enjoy Records"), "Superappin". The group went on to sign with [Sylvia Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Robinson "Sylvia Robinson")'s [Sugar Hill Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Hill_Records_(rap) "Sugar Hill Records (rap)"), following an agreement that they could perform over a then-popular DJ favorite.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

### Mainstream success and _The Message_ (1980–1982)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mainstream success and The Message (1980–1982)")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/25/Grandmaster_Flash_and_The_Furious_Five_Promotional.jpg/250px-Grandmaster_Flash_and_The_Furious_Five_Promotional.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grandmaster_Flash_and_The_Furious_Five_Promotional.jpg)

1980 promotional still of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five on mainstream success

In 1980, the group released their Sugarhill Records debut, "Freedom", which reached #19 on the R&B chart and sold over 50,000 copies.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-Grandmaster_Flash_Biography-15) The follow-up, "Birthday Party" was also a hit.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-Grandmaster_Flash_Biography-15) In 1981, Grandmaster Flash released _[The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Adventures\_of\_Grandmaster\_Flash\_on\_the\_Wheels\_of\_Steel "The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel")_, which was a multi-deck, live recording of one of his routines that featured [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(band) "Queen (band)")'s "[Another One Bites the Dust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Another_One_Bites_the_Dust "Another One Bites the Dust")" and [Chic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chic_(band) "Chic (band)")'s "[Good Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Times_(Chic_song) "Good Times (Chic song)")". The release marked the first time that scratching & turntablism were featured on a record.

In 1982, the group released "[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five song)")", which was produced by [Clifton "Jiggs" Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton_%22Jiggs%22_Chase "Clifton \"Jiggs\" Chase") and Ed "Duke Bootee" Fletcher, the latter of whom wrote the song (Sylvia Robinson added Melle Mel's rhyme from an earlier song to complete the recording). It provided a [political](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_criticism "Political criticism") and [social commentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_commentary "Social commentary") and went on to become a driving force behind [conscious hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscious_hip-hop "Conscious hip-hop"). The song peaked at #4 in the R&B chart and #62 in the pop chart, and established hip-hop's credibility in mainstream music. Other than Melle Mel, however, no members of the group (except for background vocals at the end) actually feature on the record.

Their debut album, also named _[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Message\_(Grandmaster\_Flash\_and\_the\_Furious\_Five\_album) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five album)")_, went on to become a prominent achievement in the history of hip-hop.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

### Breakup (1983–1986)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Breakup (1983–1986)")]

In 1983, Grandmaster Flash, who had never appeared on any of the group's studio recordings, sued Sugar Hill Records for $5 million in unpaid royalties. This resulted in the single "[White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Lines_(Don't_Don't_Do_It) "White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)")" being credited to "Grandmaster & Melle Mel." The song reached #47 in [_Billboard_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")'s[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_R&B/Hip-Hop_Songs "Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs") chart. Another lawsuit was filed over certain elements of the song being stolen from "Cavern" by [Liquid Liquid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Liquid "Liquid Liquid"), from which Sugar Hill Records would never recover.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-16)

The royalties dispute split the group. Melle Mel, Scorpio and Cowboy left after "White Lines (Don't Don't Do It)" was a hit. They formed Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five and released the album _Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five_ in 1984. Meanwhile, Grandmaster Flash, Kidd Creole and Rahiem left for [Elektra Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elektra_Records "Elektra Records") and added three new members to the group: Kevin "The Lord LaVon" Dukes, Russell "Mr. Broadway" Wheeler and "Larry-Love" Parker. They worked under the name "Grandmaster Flash" on _[They Said It Couldn't Be Done](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/They\_Said\_It\_Couldn't\_Be\_Done "They Said It Couldn't Be Done")_, _[The Source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Source\_(Grandmaster\_Flash\_album) "The Source (Grandmaster Flash album)")_ and _[Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang "Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang")_. The additional members The Lord La Von, Larry Love and Mr. Broadway formed the "Furious Five" but they could not use the name as Sugar Hill Records owned the rights.

Grandmaster Flash and his new "Furious Five" had a few hits with their three albums that made it to the top fifty of _Billboard_'s [R&B/Hip-Hop Albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_R&B/Hip-Hop_Albums "Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums") chart, whereas [Melle Mel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melle_Mel "Melle Mel") and his group fared better. Grandmaster Melle Mel's most notable hit was "Beat Street Breakdown", which peaked at #8 in the R&B chart. Melle Mel also appeared in [Chaka Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaka_Khan "Chaka Khan")'s "[I Feel for You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Feel_for_You "I Feel for You")", which won the [Grammy Award for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Female_R&B_Vocal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance") in 1985.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

### Reunion and waning popularity (1987–1988)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Reunion and waning popularity (1987–1988)")]

In 1987, the original lineup of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five reformed for a performance at a charity concert at Madison Square Garden. They soon reunited for their first studio album in nearly five years, recording _[On the Strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_the\_Strength "On the Strength")_, which was released in April 1988. Reception of the album was lukewarm, and it failed to achieve the same levels of success as _[The Message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Message\_(Grandmaster\_Flash\_and\_the\_Furious\_Five\_album) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five album)")_. The group never enjoyed the same success as they did in the early 1980s and permanently broke up afterwards.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

### Permanent disbandment and post-_On the Strength_ (1989–2022)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Permanent disbandment and post-On the Strength (1989–2022)")]

Since disbanding, some members of the group have briefly worked together. Melle Mel, Scorpio and Cowboy released another album as Grandmaster Melle Mel and the Furious Five, _Piano_, in 1989. Keith "Cowboy" Wiggins died on September 8, 1989.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-17)

In 1990, Grandmaster Flash produced Just-Ice's album _[Masterpiece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterpiece\_(Just-Ice\_album) "Masterpiece (Just-Ice album)")_. He went on to work as musical director for _[The Chris Rock Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Chris\_Rock\_Show "The Chris Rock Show")_, and later released _[The Official Adventures of Grandmaster Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Official\_Adventures\_of\_Grandmaster\_Flash "The Official Adventures of Grandmaster Flash")_, _[Essential Mix: Classic Edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential\_Mix:\_Classic\_Edition "Essential Mix: Classic Edition")_ and _[The Bridge (Concept of a Culture)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bridge\_(Concept\_of\_a\_Culture) "The Bridge (Concept of a Culture)")_. He has also received many accolades, including the DJ Vanguard Award from [Bill Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates") in 2004, [RIAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA "RIAA")'s Lifetime Achievement Award at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum in 2005, and [BET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BET "BET")'s [I Am Hip-Hop Icon Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BET_Hip_Hop_Awards#2006_BET_Hip_Hop_Awards_winners "BET Hip Hop Awards") in 2006. His autobiography, _The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash: My Life, My Beats_, was released in 2008.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-18)

In 1985, Melle Mel met [Quincy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Jones "Quincy Jones") at the Grammys, and they began to collaborate for _[Back on the Block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back\_on\_the\_Block "Back on the Block")_. This led to Mel being featured in the song "Back on the Block", which won him the [Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Rap_Performance_by_a_Duo_or_Group "Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group") in 1991. He would pick up an additional [Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Spoken_Word_Album "Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album") in 2002 for his contributions in _Q: The Autobiography of Quincy Jones._ 1997 saw him sign onto Straight Game Records and release _[Right Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right\_Now\_(Melle\_Mel\_album) "Right Now (Melle Mel album)")_ with Mr. Ness/Scorpio. The album also featured Rondo; the two went on to form a group called _Die Hard_. In 2012, they released an album titled _On Lock_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-interview-19)

On January 23, 2007, Mel changed his name to Grandmaster Melle Mel and released his first solo studio album, _[Muscles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscles\_(album) "Muscles (album)")_. The first single and music video was "M3 – The New Message". He has also released the children's book _The Portal in the Park_, which features a CD on which children can read and rap along with him. This project featured a then-unknown [Lady Gaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Gaga "Lady Gaga"). She performs with Mel on the songs "World Family Tree" and "The Fountain Of Truth".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-rollingstone-2)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-oldschool-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-VH1-14)

When asked of a possible reunion in 2002, Melle Mel responded:

> It['s] not a question of whether we could get together or not [...] I just don['t] think that we could get a deal. The record company people just don['t] see a market for us.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-interview-19)

However, 2014 saw Melle Mel and Scorpio begin playing shows across the United States, UK and Europe as Grandmaster's Furious Five ft Melle [sic] and Scorpio, culminating in them writing and recording new music. Their first single 'Some Kind of Sorry' was released on May 27, 2016,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-Jammerzine-20) to coincide with a UK and European tour, which they are undertaking alongside [The Sugarhill Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sugarhill_Gang "The Sugarhill Gang").

On August 2, 2017, Nathaniel Glover (Kidd Creole) was arrested and charged with the murder of a New York city homeless man.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-nyt-creole-murder-8)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-22) In 2022, Glover was found guilty of manslaughter in relation to the case, and was sentenced to sixteen years in prison.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-24)

## Legacy and influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legacy and influence")]

Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five are a well-respected group in the history of hip-hop music. They have been honored at the VH1 Hip Hop Honors in 2005 and were inducted into the [Rock & Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_&_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock & Roll Hall of Fame") in 2007. The Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. displays in their historical archives the vinyl records and the turntable used by DJ Grandmaster Flash.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-25) In 2021, they received their first [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") for [lifetime achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award"), becoming the second hip-hop act to receive the Grammy after [Run-DMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run-DMC "Run-DMC").

They have influenced many musical acts[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-26) such as [Anthony Kiedis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Kiedis "Anthony Kiedis"), [New Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Order_(band) "New Order (band)"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five#cite_note-27)[The Cold Crush Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cold_Crush_Brothers "The Cold Crush Brothers"), [Run-D.M.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run-D.M.C. "**The Message**" is a song by the American [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") group Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five. It was released as a single by [Sugar Hill Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Hill_Records_(rap) "Sugar Hill Records (rap)") on July 1, 1982, and was later featured on the group's [debut studio album of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_album) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five album)"). The song was first written in 1980 by rappers [Duke Bootee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Bootee "Duke Bootee") and Melle Mel in response to the [1980 New York City transit strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_New_York_City_transit_strike "1980 New York City transit strike"), which is mentioned in the song's lyrics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-:0-3)

"The Message" was an early prominent [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") song to provide social commentary. The song's lyrics describe the stress of inner-city poverty. In the final verses, a child born in the ghetto without prospects in life is lured away into a life of crime, for which he is jailed until he commits suicide in his cell.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-4) The song ends with a brief skit in which the band members are arrested for no clear reason.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-:0-3)

"The Message" took rap music from the house parties of its origin to the social platforms later developed by groups like [Public Enemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Enemy_(band) "Public Enemy (band)") and [KRS-One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KRS-One "KRS-One"). [Melle Mel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melle_Mel "Melle Mel") said in an interview with [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR"): "Our group, like Flash and the Furious Five, we didn't actually want to do 'The Message' because we was used to doing party raps and boasting how good we are and all that."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-5)

Commercially, it reached number 62 in the United States and made the year-end charts in the Netherlands and Australia.

## Reception

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: Reception")]

### Accolades and usage in media

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section's source code: Accolades and usage in media")]

The song was ranked as number 1 "Track of the Year" for 1982 by _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-6)

In 2004, _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked "The Message" No. 51 in its list of the [500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time"). It had the highest position for any 1980s release and was the highest-ranking hip-hop song on the list.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-7) In 2012, the publication named it the greatest hip-hop song of all time.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-8) In 2025, the song was ranked number 16 on _Rolling Stone_'s "The 100 Best Protest Songs of All Time" list.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-9)

It was voted No. 3 on [About.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About.com "About.com")'s Top 100 Rap Songs, after [Common](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_(rapper) "Common (rapper)")'s "[I Used to Love H.E.R.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Used_to_Love_H.E.R. "I Used to Love H.E.R.")" and [the Sugarhill Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sugarhill_Gang "The Sugarhill Gang")'s "[Rapper's Delight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapper's_Delight "Rapper's Delight")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-10)

In 2002, its first year of archival, it was one of 50 recordings chosen by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") to be added to the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-11) the first hip hop recording ever to receive this honor.

"The Message" was number 5 on [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1")'s 100 Greatest Songs of Hip Hop.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-12)

"The Message" is number 1 on HipHopGoldenAge's Top 100 Hip Hop Songs of the 1980s".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-13)

The song was featured in the soundtrack for the video game _[Grand Theft Auto: Vice City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand\_Theft\_Auto:\_Vice\_City "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City"),_ on the in-game radio station Wildstyle _._[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-14) It was also featured in the video game _[Fuser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuser\_(video\_game) "Fuser (video game)")_.

### Music and structure

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section's source code: Music and structure")]

![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f2/Edit-clear.svg/40px-Edit-clear.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)This section **is written like a [personal reflection, personal essay, or argumentative essay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:What_Wikipedia_is_not#Wikipedia_is_not_a_publisher_of_original_thought "Wikipedia:What Wikipedia is not")** that states a Wikipedia editor's personal feelings or presents an original argument about a topic. Please [help improve it](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit) by rewriting it in an [encyclopedic style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing_better_articles#Information_style_and_tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")._(February 2020)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

Dan Cairns of _[The Sunday Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sunday\_Times "The Sunday Times")_ has described "The Message"'s musical innovation: "Where it was inarguably innovative, was in slowing the beat right down, and opening up space in the instrumentation—the music isn't so much hip-hop as noirish, nightmarish slow-[funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), stifling and claustrophobic, with [electro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electro_(music) "Electro (music)"), [dub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dub_music "Dub music") and [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") also jostling for room in the genre mix—and thereby letting the lyrics speak loud and clear". The song utilizes a mix of musical genres, and allows the beat to take a backseat to the stark lyrical content.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-15)

### Critical reception

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section's source code: Critical reception")]

Writing in _[The Boston Phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Phoenix\_(newspaper) "The Phoenix (newspaper)")_, Sally Cragin said that the "ominous descending bassline echoes the mood—detached, preoccupied, persistent—and Flash's refrain pinpoints his perilous, repressed rage."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-16)

In addition to being widely regarded as an all-time rap anthem, "The Message" has been credited by many critics as the song that catapulted [emcees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_ceremonies "Master of ceremonies") from the background to the forefront of hip hop. The focus was thus shifted from the grandmaster mixing and scratching to the thoughts and lyrics of the emcee. David Hickley wrote in 2004 that "The Message" also crystallized a critical shift within rap itself. It confirmed that emcees, or rappers, had vaulted past the deejays as the stars of the music".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-17) In 2022, it was included in the list "The story of _NME_ in 70 (mostly) seminal songs", at number 20: [Mark Beaumont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Beaumont_(journalist) "Mark Beaumont (journalist)") wrote that with this song, "the invigorating grooves of this early breakout rap hit laid the foundations for the [...] hip-hop wars to come".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-18)

## Uses in popular culture

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section's source code: Uses in popular culture")]

The rhythm track has been [sampled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(music) "Sampling (music)") in various hip hop songs, including [Sinbad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinbad_(entertainer) "Sinbad (entertainer)")'s 1990 comedy song "Brain Damaged", the remix for the 1993 song "[Check Yo Self](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Check_Yo_Self "Check Yo Self")" by [Ice Cube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_Cube "Ice Cube"),[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-31) the 1997 song "[Can't Nobody Hold Me Down](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can't_Nobody_Hold_Me_Down "Can't Nobody Hold Me Down")" by [Puff Daddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puff_Daddy "Puff Daddy"),[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-32) the 2011 song "Teen Pregnancy" by [Blank Banshee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blank_Banshee "Blank Banshee"), and the 2022 song "[Players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Players_(Coi_Leray_song) "Players (Coi Leray song)")" by [Coi Leray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coi_Leray "Coi Leray").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-33)

On the DVD _The [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis\_(band) "Genesis (band)") Songbook_, the band and producer [Hugh Padgham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Padgham "Hugh Padgham") revealed that the inspiration for [Phil Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Collins "Phil Collins")' menacing laugh on their 1983 song "[Mama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mama_(Genesis_song) "Mama (Genesis song)")" came from "The Message".

The refrain beginning with "Don't push me 'cuz I'm close to the edge" was referenced in the animated movie _[Happy Feet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy\_Feet "Happy Feet")_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-34)

A line from the song was sampled in "Movement in Still Life" by [BT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BT_(musician) "BT (musician)"), the title track from his 1999 album _[Movement in Still Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement\_in\_Still\_Life "Movement in Still Life")_.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-35)

In 2005, a mural inspired by "The Message" was painted in the [Newtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtown,_New_South_Wales "Newtown, New South Wales") neighbourhood of [Sydney, Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney,_Australia "Sydney, Australia") by artist Colin Bebe. "It's Like a Jungle Sometimes" depicts the streets of Newtown as a literal jungle, with animals roaming the streets and swinging from poles, as a commentary on the artist's mental health and struggle with suicideality. In September 2017, [street art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_art "Street art")-based [advertising agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertising_agency "Advertising agency") Apparition Media painted over it with a mural promoting the film _[Mother!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother! "Mother!")_, featuring a giant portrait of [Jennifer Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Lawrence "Jennifer Lawrence") and the caption "#mothermovie."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-36) Much public outrage followed, as the mural had become much-loved in the community. Within hours, it had been graffitied by someone who added: "Fuck off! It really is a jungle sometimes. No respect!"[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-37) Apparition Media apologised and word of the incident also reached _Mother!'_ s director, [Darren Aronofsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darren_Aronofsky "Darren Aronofsky"), who tweeted that he was "embarrassed and furious" and would pay for the mural to be restored. It was restored in December 2017.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-38)

A reference to the lyrics was included in the song Cabinet Battle #1 from the 2015 musical [_Hamilton_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_(musical) "Hamilton (musical)").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-39)

In 2007, the 25th anniversary of "The Message", [Melle Mel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melle_Mel "Melle Mel") changed the spelling of his first name to Mele Mel and released "M3 - The New Message" as the first single to his first ever solo album, _Muscles_. 2007 was also the year that Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five became the first [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music "Hip hop music") act ever to be inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-40)

A Swedish translation/adaptation of the song, "Budskapet", was released by [Timbuktu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbuktu_(artist) "Timbuktu (artist)") in May 2013, following the [riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_2013_Stockholm_riots "May 2013 Stockholm riots") in [Husby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husby,_Stockholm "Husby, Stockholm") and other suburbs of Stockholm.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-43)

"**The Message**" is a song by the American [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") group Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five. It was released as a single by [Sugar Hill Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Hill_Records_(rap) "Sugar Hill Records (rap)") on July 1, 1982, and was later featured on the group's [debut studio album of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_album) "The Message (Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five album)"). The song was first written in 1980 by rappers [Duke Bootee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Bootee "Duke Bootee") and Melle Mel in response to the [1980 New York City transit strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_New_York_City_transit_strike "1980 New York City transit strike"), which is mentioned in the song's lyrics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-:0-3)

"The Message" was an early prominent [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") song to provide social commentary. The song's lyrics describe the stress of inner-city poverty. In the final verses, a child born in the ghetto without prospects in life is lured away into a life of crime, for which he is jailed until he commits suicide in his cell.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-4) The song ends with a brief skit in which the band members are arrested for no clear reason.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-:0-3)

"The Message" took rap music from the house parties of its origin to the social platforms later developed by groups like [Public Enemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Enemy_(band) "Public Enemy (band)") and [KRS-One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KRS-One "KRS-One"). [Melle Mel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melle_Mel "Melle Mel") said in an interview with [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR"): "Our group, like Flash and the Furious Five, we didn't actually want to do 'The Message' because we was used to doing party raps and boasting how good we are and all that."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-5)

Commercially, it reached number 62 in the United States and made the year-end charts in the Netherlands and Australia.

## Reception

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: Reception")]

### Accolades and usage in media

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section's source code: Accolades and usage in media")]

The song was ranked as number 1 "Track of the Year" for 1982 by _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-6)

In 2004, _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked "The Message" No. 51 in its list of the [500 Greatest Songs of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Songs_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time"). It had the highest position for any 1980s release and was the highest-ranking hip-hop song on the list.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-7) In 2012, the publication named it the greatest hip-hop song of all time.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-8) In 2025, the song was ranked number 16 on _Rolling Stone_'s "The 100 Best Protest Songs of All Time" list.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-9)

It was voted No. 3 on [About.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About.com "About.com")'s Top 100 Rap Songs, after [Common](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_(rapper) "Common (rapper)")'s "[I Used to Love H.E.R.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Used_to_Love_H.E.R. "I Used to Love H.E.R.")" and [the Sugarhill Gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sugarhill_Gang "The Sugarhill Gang")'s "[Rapper's Delight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapper's_Delight "Rapper's Delight")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-10)

In 2002, its first year of archival, it was one of 50 recordings chosen by the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") to be added to the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-11) the first hip hop recording ever to receive this honor.

"The Message" was number 5 on [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1")'s 100 Greatest Songs of Hip Hop.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-12)

"The Message" is number 1 on HipHopGoldenAge's Top 100 Hip Hop Songs of the 1980s".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-13)

The song was featured in the soundtrack for the video game _[Grand Theft Auto: Vice City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand\_Theft\_Auto:\_Vice\_City "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City"),_ on the in-game radio station Wildstyle _._[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-14) It was also featured in the video game _[Fuser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuser\_(video\_game) "Fuser (video game)")_.

### Music and structure

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section's source code: Music and structure")]

Please [help improve it](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit) by rewriting it in an [encyclopedic style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing_better_articles#Information_style_and_tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")._(February 2020)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

Dan Cairns of _[The Sunday Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sunday\_Times "The Sunday Times")_ has described "The Message"'s musical innovation: "Where it was inarguably innovative, was in slowing the beat right down, and opening up space in the instrumentation—the music isn't so much hip-hop as noirish, nightmarish slow-[funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), stifling and claustrophobic, with [electro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electro_(music) "Electro (music)"), [dub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dub_music "Dub music") and [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco") also jostling for room in the genre mix—and thereby letting the lyrics speak loud and clear". The song utilizes a mix of musical genres, and allows the beat to take a backseat to the stark lyrical content.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-15)

### Critical reception

[[edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section's source code: Critical reception")]

Writing in _[The Boston Phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Phoenix\_(newspaper) "The Phoenix (newspaper)")_, Sally Cragin said that the "ominous descending bassline echoes the mood—detached, preoccupied, persistent—and Flash's refrain pinpoints his perilous, repressed rage."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-16)

In addition to being widely regarded as an all-time rap anthem, "The Message" has been credited by many critics as the song that catapulted [emcees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_ceremonies "Master of ceremonies") from the background to the forefront of hip hop. The focus was thus shifted from the grandmaster mixing and scratching to the thoughts and lyrics of the emcee. David Hickley wrote in 2004 that "The Message" also crystallized a critical shift within rap itself. It confirmed that emcees, or rappers, had vaulted past the deejays as the stars of the music".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-17) In 2022, it was included in the list "The story of _NME_ in 70 (mostly) seminal songs", at number 20: [Mark Beaumont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Beaumont_(journalist) "Mark Beaumont (journalist)") wrote that with this song, "the invigorating grooves of this early breakout rap hit laid the foundations for the [...] hip-hop wars to come".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Message_(Grandmaster_Flash_and_the_Furious_Five_song)#cite_note-18)
